text:
A Decision Is Not the Same as the Capability to Act

Two households receive the same energy-price shock and make the same rational response: they cut consumption. One absorbs it — savings buffer it, an efficient home limits it, remote work removes its worst edge. The other cannot: savings deplete, retraining is deferred, work ends early. Identical behaviour. Different economy.

Economics sees the decision very well. It is largely blind to the structural conditions that determined which decisions were available in the first place.

Today The Global Structure Network publishes the expanded institutional edition of The Household Affordability Frontier. It defines the structural threshold at which the combined financial, temporal, physical and participation costs of household life begin to restrict the capacity to accumulate and deploy productive capability — and connects three domains usually examined separately: household structural conditions, monetary transmission and heterogeneous-agent dynamics, and the allocation of long-duration capital.

For central banks, institutional investors, infrastructure capital and economic strategy teams, the practical question is straightforward: which structural costs are currently preventing existing capability from becoming productive capacity, and which forms of investment can measurably expand the residual space in which households can adapt?

The framework does not claim empirical superiority over existing approaches. It is offered as a proposed analytical architecture, not a finished model — with explicit measurement requirements, testable hypotheses and clear falsification conditions published in full. If threshold position and duration below it carry no predictive power beyond income and balance sheets, the framework fails.

What is stated here can be tested — by design.

Australia has long had a really egalitarian culture with a firm anti-authoritarian streak, and a dislike of showy, pretentious speech, or self aggrandisement of any kind. Americans tend to have a different aesthetic. 
The first de-facto Australian national anthem "Waltzing Matilda"  was literally about a homeless guy who steals a sheep then commits suicide to avoid arrest.  This is not a hero-worshipping culture. 

A significant minority of our foundation stock was Irish, and we had Irish political prisoners incarcerated here to get them out of the UK from early Colonial times. This combined readily with an ex-convict minority who had a deep seated mistrust of authority , exemplified by characters like Ned Kelly. 
But a more general cynicism  towards the aristocratic, British part of Ausralian society that included many leading business figures and large institutional concerns remained, and the later Socialist mistrust of Elites transferred easily to "bosses" of any sort. 
Australia's organised labour movements and Fabianism have greatly influenced Australian culture and political aesthetics, if not always  actual policy; even as many of the  Australian business leaders who emerged post-War were entirely self-made, including literal refugees like the Smorgon family who built steel mills and the Meyers who built the leading department stores - there remained a strong feeling against the "Big End of Town" more generally. As British capital declined, American companies came to take their place, and certainly inherited some of that left-wing antipathy. 

Australia has fought for Britain in every conflict from the Boer War until Korea, entering years before the US in both world wars and losing staggering numbers of men relative to population. The soldiers were volunteers in most cases and like most Commonwealth troops had positively miserable wages and rough conditions compared to the Americans . 

Particularly in WW2 there was a lot of resentlent from Australian troops returning home after many years of war to find Americans who earned five times their salaries and had access to then-unobtainable consumer products fron US stores like stockings and chocolate- making free with the Aussies' wives and girlfriends while on leave in Australian port cities. There were significant brawls over this between large groups of soldiers on leave at times. 

"Overpaid, oversexed and over here" was the joke about this time.

I would argue though that none of this amounts to actual hatred in most cases. Australia does have an extremely sharp sense of humour that is never happier than when cutting down "tall poppies". Americans are therefore seen as the legitimate butt of jokes, and the unfortunate sneering sort of humour that Social Studdies teachers encourage their little sheep to engage in. But this is not hatred. 

Labor policies, have rejected revolutionary forms of socialism, but keep Socialist policy objectives; these are sought via  Government spending, rather than radical change. The ideas of Keynesian Stim and "MMT" offered them a black checkbook post 2007 and the resulting public sector expansion created enormous bureaucratic structures, that employ nearly one-fifth of the population; another one-third are on some sort of pension or support. This is reflected in a widespread ambivalence towards business from large portions of the population. State schooling, with strong teachers' unions, make sure that these political aesthetics are transferred to the young. 

In spite of all this, I think actual hate towards Americans is rare. Quite scathing humour is common, but Aussies don't spare each other from that either so it shouldn't be taken too personally. 

Australia does have a strong Conservative backbone as well; Australia's conservatives appreciate US very much indeed and absolutely adore it when they travel there. In fairness most of the lefties ("Pinkos" in Aussie slang, they don't escape a nickname either) love it too if they go.

The Night the Otherworld Opened — The Adventure of Nera

In medieval Irish literature, Samhain was a time when the ordinary world and the Otherworld could meet.

On Samhain Eve, King Ailill and Queen Medb hold a feast at their royal stronghold of Ráth Cruachan in Connacht.

Two captives have been hanged outside, and Ailill offers a reward to anyone brave enough to approach them and fasten a twig around the foot of one of the hanged men. One by one, the men venture into the darkness, but none succeeds.

Then Nera steps forward.

As he approaches the gallows, one of the dead men speaks to him and asks to be carried on his back to find a drink. Nera takes him to three houses, encountering strange and terrifying obstacles along the way, before returning him to the gallows.

When he finally returns to Cruachan, he sees a vision of the royal stronghold in ruins, its people apparently slain.

He follows a mysterious host into a cave and finds himself in the Otherworld.

There he discovers a strange kingdom where time passes differently. After what seems to him like three days and three nights, a woman of the Otherworld reveals that the destruction of Cruachan was a vision of an attack yet to come. She sends him back to warn his people, though in their world the feast has barely progressed.

As proof of his journey, he brings back the fruits of summer: wild garlic, primrose and golden fern.

The tale concludes with the extraordinary fate of Nera, who remains in the Otherworld until Doomsday.
